I would keep it simple and stay with the cropping pattern I know best: winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same land. In Quzhou County, that is the most reliable way for me to use a full year, spread risk, and make use of the irrigation, labor, and machines that are commonly available. At my age, I would not choose a crop that needs a lot of hand work or complicated management. I would rather grow crops I understand well, that I can manage on time, and that I know I can sell.

For seed, I would use improved seed instead of traditional seed because I want steadier yield and better stand establishment, but I would avoid anything that feels too risky or unfamiliar. For wheat, I would focus on getting a strong stand, applying fertilizer in a steady way, irrigating at the key times, and controlling weeds and disease before they spread. After wheat harvest, I would move straight into summer maize so I do not lose soil moisture or miss the planting window. For maize, I would keep the field clean, feed it enough nitrogen for strong growth, and give one or two irrigations depending on rainfall. I would not overcomplicate the plan. I would rely on a familiar wheat-maize rotation, moderate fertilizer, timely water, and a limited number of pesticide sprays only when needed, because that is the way I would protect yield while keeping the work manageable.
